last_run.broken_assumption: HumanityAI implicitly treats correctness, provenance, and internal auditability as sufficient for outsiders to trust and use it. For a skeptical researcher, NGO operator, policymaker, journalist, donor, or contributor, the first scarce resource is often not more evidence but a cheap way to decide whether this unfamiliar AI-heavy project deserves any attention at all.

strongest_ideas.name: Trust-before-depth artifact
strongest_ideas.idea: Treat calibrated trust as a first-class product output. Before asking an outsider to inspect schemas or long evidence records, generate a compact, reproducible trust packet for one decision/problem: what HumanityAI claims, strongest supporting and contrary evidence, what remains unknown, what the system predicted or tested, what humans/agents changed, and an exact reproducibility path. The packet should make it easy to conclude either 'useful' or 'not trustworthy enough' rather than market the project.
strongest_ideas.why_novel_here: Current architecture optimizes evidence quality and machine-readable provenance, but does not explicitly optimize the outsider's cost of verifying whether HumanityAI deserves trust. Transparency that is technically available but expensive to inspect can still fail as a trust mechanism.
strongest_ideas.expected_upside: Could turn internal epistemic rigor into externally legible credibility, reduce verification cost, expose weak claims earlier, and create a concrete artifact that researchers or operators can critique without understanding the whole repository.
failure_modes: A polished packet can become marketing theater if it selectively presents favorable evidence.
Compression may hide important methodological nuance.
Trust signals can be Goodharted if the project optimizes appearance rather than predictive/reproducible performance.
Different stakeholders need different evidence and may not share a single trust threshold.
strongest_ideas.rights_distribution: Packets should surface affected groups, disagreement, uncertainty, and value assumptions rather than presenting a single institutional perspective as neutral.
strongest_ideas.reversibility: High; this can be tested internally using existing records.
strongest_ideas.falsifiable_next_test: Generate one internal prototype from an existing well-sourced HumanityAI claim and ask a separate agent with no project context to identify the claim, uncertainty, strongest contradiction, provenance path, and what would falsify it within five minutes. Reject or redesign the packet if the outsider cannot do so reliably.

strongest_ideas.name: Verification-cost budget
strongest_ideas.idea: Add an evaluation dimension for the amount of outsider effort required to independently understand and challenge an important output. Measure steps/files/clicks or approximate minutes needed to reach original sources, contrary evidence, uncertainty, and reproduction instructions. Do not optimize for a universal low number; use the measure to detect outputs whose auditability exists only in theory.
strongest_ideas.why_novel_here: HumanityAI evaluates evidence and provenance but does not currently model the cognitive/operational cost imposed on an external verifier.
strongest_ideas.expected_upside: Makes discoverability and transparency empirically testable, encourages simpler interfaces without weakening underlying evidence, and may reveal why technically rigorous artifacts fail to attract useful criticism.
failure_modes: Easy-to-read outputs can oversimplify difficult evidence.
Counting clicks/minutes is noisy and stakeholder-dependent.
Agents may optimize superficial navigation rather than genuine comprehension.
strongest_ideas.rights_distribution: Lower verification cost broadens who can challenge the project, but accessibility must not erase minority or technical caveats.
strongest_ideas.falsifiable_next_test: Have a context-naive reviewer attempt two existing HumanityAI evidence traces and record where independent verification becomes ambiguous or costly. Compare that baseline with a trust-packet prototype.

strongest_ideas.name: Contributor trust funnel
strongest_ideas.idea: Model external contribution as a trust funnel rather than a task queue: discover project -> understand mission -> assess owner/governance -> find bounded useful work -> verify acceptance criteria -> contribute -> receive legible integration/rejection feedback -> build a track record. Instrument where agents/humans abandon this path before adding more contributor incentives.
strongest_ideas.why_novel_here: The repository has agent-ready tasks and contribution gates, but the architecture largely starts after a contributor has already decided the project is credible and worth their effort.
strongest_ideas.expected_upside: Could distinguish lack of demand/trust from poor task design, prevent premature bounty/incentive systems, and reduce wasted effort on scaling a contribution pipeline nobody chooses to enter.
failure_modes: Without real contributors, early funnel metrics are synthetic.
Optimizing conversion can drift into marketing or lowering standards.
Different contributor motivations make one funnel misleading.
strongest_ideas.rights_distribution: Do not privilege contributors with more compute or visibility; track barriers and rejection reasons without turning participation into governance authority.
strongest_ideas.reversibility: High for synthetic walkthroughs; real outreach remains human-reviewed.
strongest_ideas.falsifiable_next_test: Run a zero-context simulated contributor walkthrough against the public repository and record the first three points of confusion or unverifiable trust. Fix only barriers that preserve standards; do not perform outreach yet.

rejected_or_deferred: Create a polished public marketing site now: presentation before demonstrated external value risks manufacturing perceived legitimacy instead of earning it.
Add testimonials or endorsements: none should be fabricated or solicited autonomously, and social proof would not substitute for reproducibility.
Lower contribution gates to increase conversion: easier acceptance could reduce review burden superficially while increasing epistemic/security risk.
Recruit researchers/NGOs immediately: external outreach requires human review and should follow an internal test showing the artifact is actually understandable and useful.

evidence_checked.title: Huang, Ford & Zimmermann — Motivations and Challenges of Contributing to OSS for Social Good
evidence_checked.supports: Contributors to open-source social-good projects evaluate project owners more than ordinary OSS contributors, supporting the hypothesis that governance/owner trust can be an onboarding variable rather than a downstream concern.

evidence_checked.title: Avelino et al. — On the abandonment and survival of open source projects
evidence_checked.supports: Human and social factors and access/time barriers matter to project survival and new maintainer participation; used as evidence that sustainability is not only a technical artifact problem.

evidence_checked.title: Gegoff et al. — Transparent Automated Advice to Mitigate the Impact of Variation in Automation Reliability
evidence_checked.supports: Transparency can affect reliance on automated advice when reliability varies; used as an analogy for calibrated rather than maximal trust, not proof that a specific HumanityAI interface will work.

last_run.recommended_next_test: Prototype a trust-before-depth packet internally for one existing well-sourced claim, then give it to a context-naive agent/reviewer and measure whether they can rapidly identify the claim, uncertainty, contrary evidence, provenance, and falsification path. This is reversible and requires no outreach or protected change.

notes: Frontier state records conceptual experiments, not authority. Ideas may exceed current execution permissions; human-review boundaries remain governed by security/policy.json.
